title: Targets, pointing, touch, and motor effort
outcome: Design controls that are easy to reach and distinguish, beyond making icons larger.
useCase: Dense toolbars, table actions, and mobile operational screens.
benefits: Reduces avoidable motor errors and missed controls.
drawbacks: Space is limited; target design must balance density and task needs.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Make the intended action easy to hit and hard to confuse.

trace.title: Intended action
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Fitts’s law connects pointing movement difficulty with target distance and size in a given task. The practical cue is useful: tiny distant targets are often harder to acquire.

It does not mean every primary button should fill the entire screen.

The hit area matters, not just the visible icon. Spacing helps users distinguish adjacent actions and avoid accidental taps.

Destructive and routine actions should not be indistinguishable neighbors. Keyboard access supplies another path; it does not excuse unusable pointer targets.

Consider touch, mouse, zoom, one-handed use, and limited motor control. A hover-only action can be unavailable on touch and hard to discover.

Use WCAG target-size guidance with its exceptions and context rather than treating a single pixel number as the whole usability test.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Point at the intended target → move → acquire it → confirm the outcome. Watch misclicks and corrective movement.

Then complete the same task with keyboard focus and a narrow touch screen.

When a target moves after the user starts pointing because an image loads above it, size alone will not fix the error. Stable layout is part of target reliability.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: A large icon inside a tiny clickable wrapper can still have a small target. A tooltip-only accessible name can be absent for keyboard or touch users.
